1373.title: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram
1373.hook: a father finds milk on his small son's lips and demands to know who fed him
1373.howItsDone: Sambandar's hymns are sung by oduvars, the singers of Tamil Shaiva temples, and the story of the milk at the temple tank is told at Sirkazhi, the town of his birth.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Appar, the singer with a hoe, sent a king a song instead of himself: we are subjects of no one.
screen: `SUBJECTS OF NO ONE.`

segments.voice: Who gave you this milk? A father stands over his small son on the steps of a temple tank, and he's angry. He went down into the water to bathe and left the boy on the bank. Now he's come up, there's milk on the child's lips, and nobody else in sight. He raises a stick. Who fed you? The boy doesn't cry or make an excuse. He lifts his hand, points up at the sky, and starts to sing. Today, another of the Tevaram's three singers: Sambandar.
screen: `WHO GAVE YOU THIS MILK?` → `A SMALL BOY POINTS UP.` → `AND STARTS TO SING.`

segments.voice: The Periya Puranam tells it, in paraphrase. The town is Sirkazhi, in the Tamil country. While his father is under the water, the child, alone, cries out for his mother and father. Shiva and the Goddess appear above the tank. She fills a golden cup with her own milk, mixed with divine wisdom, and gives it to him. Then they're gone, and the father comes up the steps. The boy's song begins, in paraphrase: the one with an earring in his ear, who rides the bull, who wears the pure white crescent moon, smeared with the ash of the burning ground, he is the thief who stole my heart. He lives here, in this town. The father asked a plain question, who fed you, and the answer is a portrait: not a name, but the earring, the bull, the moon, the ash, the way you'd describe someone you'd just seen up close. Then that phrase: the thief who stole my heart. A strange thing to call God, and a tender one. Shiva doesn't wait to be invited in. He takes the heart first, and the song comes after. And notice where the song ends: in this town, here. That's the mark of the Tevaram, a faith with a map in its scripture; even this first hymn names its place. The story says the boy went on to sing at shrine after shrine, carried on his father's shoulders at first, and the tradition remembers him as the child the Goddess fed. His father came up the steps to scold him, and went home with a hymn.
screen: `A CHILD ALONE ON THE BANK` · `MILK IN A GOLDEN CUP` · `THE THIEF WHO STOLE MY HEART` · `A HYMN THAT NAMES ITS TOWN`

segments.voice: Ask yourself quietly what has stolen your heart lately, not what ought to have, but what actually did: a face, a piece of music, a view from a window, a cause. Let it come without judging it, and notice how it feels to be taken like that, without asking. If you pray, you can ask God to be the one who steals it next.

1374.title: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram
1374.hook: a hunter brings Shiva water carried in his mouth and meat he has tasted first
1374.howItsDone: Kannappa is honored among the Nayanmars, the Shaiva saints of the Tamil country, and his story is told at the Shiva temple of Kalahasti, the hill shrine where tradition places it.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sambandar, fed by the Goddess, sang of the thief who stole his heart.
screen: `THE THIEF WHO STOLE MY HEART.`

segments.voice: Water, carried up a hill in a man's mouth, because he has no pot. Wildflowers tucked into his hair, because his hands are full. A piece of roasted meat, which he has bitten into first, to make sure it's tender and good. A young hunter climbs into a forest shrine and lays all this before Shiva. He spits the water over the stone to wash it, shakes the flowers from his hair, sets down the meat, and stands guard all night with his bow. Today, the hunter the Tamil Shaiva saints call Kannappa.
screen: `WATER CARRIED IN HIS MOUTH.` → `FLOWERS IN HIS HAIR.` → `MEAT HE TASTED FIRST.`

segments.voice: The Periya Puranam tells it, in paraphrase. The shrine already has a priest, a careful man who comes each morning with pure water and proper flowers. Each morning he finds the place littered with bones and wilted blossoms, grieves, cleans it all, and worships again. At last Shiva tells him: hide tomorrow, and watch. So the priest hides. The hunter arrives and sees something terrible: blood running from one eye of Shiva's image. He tries forest herbs. Nothing stops it. So he takes an arrow, cuts out his own eye, and presses it to the place. The bleeding stops, and he laughs with joy. Then the other eye of the image begins to bleed. Once his second eye is gone he won't be able to find the spot, so he sets his foot on it to mark the place, and raises the arrow to his face. And Shiva's hand comes out of the stone and holds his hand. Stop, Kannappa, Shiva says, and the story has him say it again. The story doesn't mock the priest. His worship was right, and Shiva honors it by letting him see a second kind of love, one that knew none of the rules and held nothing back. The foot on the sacred image, the meat, the water from a mouth: by the rules, each is wrong, and the story keeps every one. Sundarar, in a hymn listing the Lord's servants, names Kannappa among them. Even a saint who knew every rule counted the hunter as one of his own.
screen: `A PRIEST WHO GRIEVES EACH MORNING` · `THE IMAGE BEGINS TO BLEED` · `A FOOT TO MARK THE PLACE` · `STOP, KANNAPPA`

segments.voice: Think of something you'd like to give today, to someone you love, to your work, or to God if you pray. Set aside the ideal version, and look at what's really in your hands: a tired hour, a short call, a clumsy word of thanks. Let that be enough to give, the way the hunter gave, without polishing it first.

1375.title: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram
1375.hook: love and Shiva are two, say those who don't know: Tirumular's short verse
1375.howItsDone: Tirumular is honored among the Nayanmars, the Shaiva saints of the Tamil country, and the words 'anbe sivam', love is Shiva, from his verse are spoken and written by Tamil Shaivas.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kannappa, the hunter who knew none of the rules, was stopped by Shiva's own hand.
screen: `STOP, KANNAPPA.`

segments.voice: Love and Shiva are two, say those who don't know. That's the first line of a short Tamil verse, spoken by a man the tradition calls Tirumular. How he got that name is strange. A traveling yogi comes upon a herd of cows gathered around the body of their cowherd, who has just died. The cows are lowing, circling, refusing to leave him. The yogi can't bear it. So, the story says, he leaves his own body and enters the cowherd's. And the cowherd stands up.
screen: `COWS AROUND A DEAD COWHERD.` → `A YOGI CAN'T BEAR IT.` → `THE COWHERD STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the rest, as the Periya Puranam tells it, in paraphrase. The cows, comforted, go home. The yogi means to return to his own body, but when he looks for it, it's gone. Shiva's will, the story says. So he stays in the cowherd's body, under the cowherd's name, Mular, and settles down to meditate and compose the Tirumantiram, a long book of verses on Shiva and the path to him. It sits in the Tirumurai, the collection that holds the Tevaram. Now the verse, in paraphrase. Love and Shiva are two, say those who don't know. No one knows that love itself is Shiva. When they know that love itself is Shiva, they rest there, as love, as Shiva. The verse doesn't say Shiva is loving, the way you'd say a person is kind. It goes further: the love is Shiva. Not a quality he has, but who he is. Now go back to the field. The story starts with a man who couldn't bear the grief of some cows. He wasn't seeking a vision. He was moved by animals crying for their herder, and gave up his own body to comfort them. Before he wrote a single verse, he'd already done what the verse says. Looking back over these Tamil days: Appar, who belonged so wholly to Shiva that a king couldn't summon him; Sambandar, whose heart was stolen; Kannappa, who held nothing back; and a cowherd who was really a yogi, saying it plainly: love itself is Shiva.
screen: `THE BODY HE COULDN'T FIND` · `THE TIRUMANTIRAM` · `LOVE ITSELF IS SHIVA` · `HE DID IT BEFORE HE WROTE IT`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love, a person or even an animal, see their face for a moment, and feel the warmth that comes with it. Then gently let the face fade and stay with the warmth, not the person now, just the love; when the mind goes looking for the face, let it, and come back. If you pray, you can rest in the verse's words: love itself is Shiva.
Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram. Today, Tirumular, the yogi who entered a cowherd's body to comfort his cows, and whose verse says love itself is Shiva. Today's word.
screen: `TAMIL SHAIVISM AND THE TEVARAM — today's word`.

1376.title: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams
1376.hook: a conch at dusk and a drum in the street: two ways of loving God in one country
1376.howItsDone: In Bengal, Shakta devotees worship the Goddess as Durga and Kali, at home and at autumn festivals, while Vaishnava devotees gather for kirtan, singing the names of Krishna together to drum and cymbals.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tirumular, who entered a cowherd's body for the sake of grieving cows, and said love itself is Shiva.
screen: `LOVE ITSELF IS SHIVA.`

segments.voice: Dusk in a Bengali village. In one courtyard, someone lifts a conch shell, blows a long round note, and lights a lamp before a small image of the Goddess. A few lanes over, a clay drum starts up, a cymbal joins it, and a handful of people begin singing the names of Krishna, louder and faster, until a couple of them are swaying with their arms in the air. Same village, same evening, two sounds. Today we cross the subcontinent to Bengal, and two streams of devotion that run through it side by side.
screen: `A CONCH AT DUSK.` → `A DRUM IN THE NEXT LANE.` → `TWO STREAMS, ONE VILLAGE.`

segments.voice: First, the conch and the lamp. The Shakta stream worships God as the Goddess, as Shakti, the power that makes and moves everything. In Bengal she has many faces: Durga riding her lion, Kali dark and fierce. And devotees call her by the simplest name there is: Ma. Mother. A text the Shaktas treasure, the Devi Mahatmya, tells of the Goddess rising when the gods themselves can't defeat the demons, and saying, in paraphrase, that whenever trouble comes, she will come again. Now the drum. The Vaishnava stream worships Vishnu, and in Bengal, above all, Krishna, the cowherd of Vrindavan, and Radha, who loves him. Tradition says this stream was set alight by Chaitanya, a teacher from Nabadwip who led people through the streets singing the names of God together. That singing is kirtan, and it's still the heart of it: the name, sung out loud, in company. The two can sound like opposites: a fierce Mother with a sword, a flute-playing boy in a meadow. But they share a grammar. Both call God by a close family name, Mother on one side, and on the other, beloved, child, friend. Both lean on singing more than argument. And these are streams, not walls. Later this week, a priest of Kali who also wept for Krishna, and singers whose songs borrow from more than one stream. Over the next days we'll follow each stream in turn, and watch where they meet.
screen: `SHAKTI: GOD AS MOTHER` · `KRISHNA, SUNG IN THE STREETS` · `TWO STREAMS, ONE GRAMMAR` · `STREAMS, NOT WALLS`

segments.voice: Hum quietly on an out-breath, one long sound, low and round like the conch, and let it fade into silence. Then for a few breaths let the breath be quicker and lighter, like a drum starting up, before it settles again, and notice which one your body likes today. If you pray, let one name for God ride on the out-breath: Ma, or Krishna, or the name you use.
Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Two ways of devotion running side by side: the Goddess called Mother, and Krishna sung in the street. Today's word.

1377.title: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams
1377.hook: a clerk's account book fills up with songs to Kali
1377.howItsDone: Ramprasad's songs to Kali are sung in Bengal at Kali Puja, at home and in devotional gatherings, as part of the song tradition known as Shyama Sangeet.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a conch at dusk for the Goddess, and a drum in the next lane for Krishna: two streams, not walls.
screen: `STREAMS, NOT WALLS.`

segments.voice: An office in Calcutta. A young clerk is supposed to be copying figures into the account book, rows of numbers, day after day. But the other clerks notice the margins of his ledger filling up with something else: lines of verse, songs to Kali, the dark Mother. Somebody takes the book to the employer, expecting the young man to be fired. The employer opens it, starts reading, and doesn't stop. Today, the Shakta stream through one singer: Ramprasad Sen.
screen: `A CLERK AND HIS LEDGER.` → `SONGS IN THE MARGINS.` → `THE EMPLOYER READS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the employer was so moved that instead of dismissing him, he sent Ramprasad home to his village with an allowance, so he could do nothing but sing. His songs, the stories say, spread from village to village, sung by boatmen and farmers, and tradition gives a melody his name. Listen to how he talks to Kali. Not like a courtier bowing to a queen. Like a child to his mother. In one song, in paraphrase, he complains: other children have a mother who looks after them, so why am I left like this? Is this how a mother behaves? He sulks, he pleads, he threatens to tell everyone. That's the Shakta stream at its warmest. The Goddess may be fierce, with a sword and a necklace of heads, but to the singer she is Ma, and a child is allowed to be cross with his mother. People tell a story about him. He was mending a fence and needed someone to hold the rope on the other side. His young daughter came and held it. Later, when he thanked her, she said she'd been away the whole time. So who held the rope? In the story, the Mother herself, wearing a little girl's face. And his songs aren't only sweet. In one, he scolds his own mind as a lazy farmer: this human life is a good field, and you've left it lying fallow. Tend it, and gold would grow. Tender with the Mother, hard on himself. That's the voice that came out of an account book.
screen: `SONGS IN THE ACCOUNT BOOK` · `A CHILD, CROSS WITH HIS MOTHER` · `WHO HELD THE ROPE?` · `THE FIELD LEFT FALLOW`

segments.voice: Picture your day as a small plot of ground: some of it planted, things you tended and people you looked after, and some lying fallow, a thing you keep meaning to start, a call you haven't made. Walk around the field in your mind and notice, without scolding yourself. If you pray, you can call on the Mother, or on God, as the one who holds the rope on the other side.
Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams: the Shakta stream in Ramprasad Sen, the clerk who filled his ledger with songs and talked to Kali like a child to his mother. Today's word.
screen: `BENGAL'S SHAKTA AND VAISHNAVA STREAMS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Songs to the Mother, in a ledger's margins. See you tomorrow.

1378.title: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams
1378.hook: a grammar teacher comes home from pilgrimage and every word he explains turns into Krishna
1378.howItsDone: Gaudiya Vaishnavas, who follow Chaitanya, gather for kirtan, singing the names of Krishna together to the khol drum and hand cymbals, and some take the singing into the streets.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramprasad, the clerk who wrote songs to Kali in his account book, cross with his Mother and hard on himself.
screen: `THE FIELD LEFT FALLOW.`

segments.voice: What happens to a grammar lesson when the teacher can only think of God? In Nabadwip, a town of scholars on the river, the teacher is young and sharp, known for his skill in Sanskrit grammar, and his students are proud to study with him. Then he goes away on a pilgrimage, and comes back different. He sits down to explain an ordinary word, a verb, a root, and somehow the explanation ends in Krishna. The next word, the same. The students look at each other. They came for grammar. Today, the Vaishnava stream, and a teacher you met earlier on this path: Chaitanya.
screen: `A YOUNG GRAMMAR TEACHER.` → `A PILGRIMAGE.` → `EVERY WORD ENDS IN KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: The biographies tell this story, and they don't make fun of the students. In the end he closes the school. He can't teach grammar anymore, because every word has become a door to the same room. So what does he do instead? He sings. With friends, in a courtyard at first, then out in the streets of Nabadwip: the names of God, Hari, Krishna, over and over to drums and cymbals, louder and faster, until people are dancing. That's kirtan, and in this stream it isn't decoration. It is the practice: the name, sung out loud, in company. The singing could sound like showing off. But Chaitanya is remembered for a handful of short teaching verses, and one of them, in paraphrase, says how to sing: humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree, giving honor to others and wanting none for yourself. A tree, the old explanation goes, gives shade even to the one who cuts it down. So the loudest practice in the stream is meant to come from the lowest place. Remember the conch on Bengal's first day, the Goddess as Mother? The Vaishnava stream also reaches for a close name. For Chaitanya's followers the closest of all is Radha's love for Krishna, and in their stories Chaitanya himself weeps and longs for Krishna the way Radha does. The scholar who couldn't stop saying Krishna ends up singing in the street, as low as grass.
screen: `EVERY WORD BECOMES KRISHNA` · `THE NAME, SUNG IN THE STREETS` · `HUMBLER THAN A BLADE OF GRASS` · `LONGING LIKE RADHA`

segments.voice: On the in-breath, picture a blade of grass, low, bending when it's walked on, standing up again; on the out-breath, a tree, rooted, patient, giving shade. Go back and forth, grass and tree, and bring to mind one person who might need you to bend, or to wait. If you pray, let a name of God, Hari or Krishna or your own, sound softly with the breath.

1379.title: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams
1379.hook: a goddess shaped from river clay, welcomed home like a daughter, and sent back to the river
1379.howItsDone: At Durga Puja, Bengali Hindus install clay images of Durga in homes and neighborhood pavilions, worship her for the festival days, and on Vijaya Dashami immerse the image in a river or pond.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chaitanya, the grammar teacher who sang the names of Krishna in the street, humbler than a blade of grass.
screen: `HUMBLER THAN A BLADE OF GRASS.`

segments.voice: Straw, bound tight with twine into the shape of a body. Then clay from the riverbank, pressed on in layers, smoothed by thumbs, left to dry, cracked, filled, smoothed again, in workshops along the river in Bengal. Slowly a face appears: wide eyes, a calm mouth, many arms, a lion at her feet. Then paint, cloth, jewelry. By autumn she's ready, and families and neighborhoods carry her in. Today, the Shakta stream at its most public, Durga Puja, and what happens to her at the end.
screen: `STRAW AND RIVER CLAY.` → `A FACE APPEARS.` → `CARRIED IN, IN AUTUMN.`

segments.voice: The text behind Durga is the Devi Mahatmya, and it tells of her as a warrior: the gods pour their powers into her, she rides out on her lion, and defeats the buffalo demon none of them could. That's the image in the clay, spear in hand. But in Bengal the festival tells a second story at the same time. Durga is also Uma, daughter of the mountain king Himalaya and his wife Menaka. She's married to Shiva and lives far away on his mountain, and once a year she comes home to visit her parents, bringing her children. So the festival feels like a homecoming. Bengali songs called agamani, songs of arrival, put words in the mother's mouth: is my Uma really coming? How thin has she gotten? What has that husband of hers been feeding her? In Bengal, the fierce goddess and the daughter whose mother worries are one. On the last day, Vijaya, she has to go back. Married women, in a custom called sindur khela, smear red vermilion on the goddess's face and on each other, the way you'd send a daughter off. Then the image, all that patient work, is carried to the river and lowered into the water, and the clay goes back where it came from. The goodbye songs are sad, and the greeting afterward is happy: people visit, embrace, share sweets. Behind us this week: Sambandar's song, Kannappa's eye, Tirumular's cows, the conch and the drum, Ramprasad's ledger, Chaitanya's street. Now a goddess who comes home, and goes.
screen: `THE WARRIOR ON THE LION` · `UMA, THE DAUGHTER COMING HOME` · `RED VERMILION FOR GOODBYE` · `THE CLAY GOES BACK TO THE RIVER`

segments.voice: On the in-breath, think of someone you love arriving, the door opening, their face, and let yourself be glad. On the out-breath, think of letting them go again, the door closing, the car pulling away, and hold on to neither, just breathing the arriving and the leaving. If you pray, you can hold that person before the Goddess, or before God, as they come and as they go.
Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Today, Durga Puja: the warrior goddess welcomed home as Uma, the daughter, then given back to the river. Today's word.
